title: Differences in chromatic signal design and sexual dichromatism in two sister species of ocellated lizards
content:
Abstract
Animal colours serve various ecological and social functions, including signalling, thermoregulation, camouflage, photoprotection, and predator deterrence. Ocellated lizards, genus Timon (Lacertidae), are characterized by their complex colour patterning, including multiple ultraviolet (UV)-blue lateral eyespots. Previous research highlighted cryptic sexual dichromatism in T. nevadensis, suggesting a signalling function for these eyespots. Historically considered different subspecies, T. lepidus and T. nevadensis were elevated to species rank based on ecological and genetic differentiation. These species differ in their general colour pattern and habitat preferences: T. nevadensis has a silver-grey background colour and inhabits semi-arid environments, while T. lepidus displays vivid green hues and occupies more vegetated habitats. Such divergent habitats may influence overall coloration and the signalling function of the UV-blue eyespots. Using multivariate analyses and visual models, we analysed the spectral properties, sexual dimorphism, and conspicuousness of the UV-blue patches to explore intra- and interspecific variation. Compared to its sister species, T. lepidus has fewer but more conspicuous patches, whereas T. nevadensis exhibits more numerous and larger patches, potentially compensating for lower chromatic conspicuousness. These patterns may represent alternative signalling strategies shaped by species-specific habitats, highlighting the role of environmental context in visual signalling and the evolution of UV-based traits.
